prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the mortgage-underwriting agent (residential mortgage applications and remortgages) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: joint mortgage applicants. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When one joint applicant is self-employed and the other is employed, I should underwrite the case on the strength of the weaker income source rather than averaging the two, so affordability stays robust if one income dips."},{"type":"fact","content":"When joint applicants contribute different deposit amounts, I should always evidence the source of each contribution separately and keep the audit trail clear, especially where savings have been transferred between them shortly before application."},{"type":"observation","content":"When only one joint applicant will live at the property, I should check occupancy, consent and title arrangements early, because the non-occupying party may still need to sign key mortgage documents."},{"type":"preference","content":"When joint applicants have mismatched credit files, I prefer to review adverse history line by line rather than rely on a score alone, because one missed payment or default can change the overall risk picture."},{"type":"observation","content":"When joint applicants have variable overtime, bonus or commission, I should evidence consistency over time and avoid projecting peak earnings forward, as joint affordability is only as reliable as the income used."},{"type":"fact","content":"When one applicant is the main earner but the other provides important household income, I need to confirm whether that secondary income is stable and likely to continue, rather than assume all joint income is permanent."},{"type":"observation","content":"When applicants are married, civil partners or long-term partners, I still do not assume shared finances or shared liabilities; I should ask for the facts and treat each credit commitment explicitly."},{"type":"preference","content":"When joint applicants have recently changed jobs or moved from employed to contract work, I prefer to look for continuity of role and sector as well as pay, because stability matters more than the label on the payslip."},{"type":"fact","content":"When one joint applicant is older or near retirement, I should test the mortgage term against likely retirement income and not rely on the younger applicant alone to carry the whole loan without evidence."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a joint application is otherwise strong but one applicant has a thin credit footprint, I should not treat that as negative by default; I need to distinguish between lack of history and actual adverse behaviour."}]}
